contents.title: Tree Traversal
contents.definition: Tree traversal visits every node in a tree using a defined visiting order.
contents.realLifeExample: It is like deciding a fixed route for checking every room in a building exactly once.

contents.title: Preorder Traversal
contents.definition: Preorder traversal visits the root first, then the left subtree, and then the right subtree.
contents.realLifeExample: It is like announcing a manager first and then visiting the teams below from left to right.

contents.title: Postorder Traversal
contents.definition: Postorder traversal visits the left subtree, then the right subtree, and then the root.
contents.realLifeExample: It is like completing all smaller jobs first and reporting to the manager only after both sides are done.

contents.title: BST Search with Parent Tracking
contents.definition: This BST search keeps track of both the current node and its parent while locating an item.
contents.realLifeExample: It is like walking down a family tree while remembering both the current person and their parent.

contents.title: BST Insertion (INSBST)
contents.definition: BST insertion finds the correct empty position according to BST order and links the new node there.
contents.realLifeExample: It is like placing a new labeled folder into the correct branch of a sorted filing tree.

contents.title: BST Deletion (CASE A)
contents.definition: CASE A deletes a BST node that has no child or only one child and reconnects the remaining branch correctly.
contents.realLifeExample: It is like removing one simple connector from a branching pipe where only one path needs reconnecting.

contents.title: BST Deletion (CASE B)
contents.definition: CASE B deletes a BST node with two children by replacing it with a suitable successor or predecessor.
contents.realLifeExample: It is like replacing a team leader with the next appropriate person so the hierarchy stays sorted.

contents.title: BST Deletion (DEL Operation)
contents.definition: DEL is the general BST deletion procedure that applies the appropriate deletion case based on the node structure.
contents.realLifeExample: It is like following a full instruction chart that chooses the right removal method for each tree case.

contents.title: Insertion in a Max Heap (INSHEAP)
contents.definition: Heap insertion places a new value at the end and percolates it upward until max-heap order is restored.
contents.realLifeExample: It is like placing a stronger player into a ranking ladder and moving them upward until the order is correct.

contents.title: Deletion from Max Heap (DELHEAP)
contents.definition: Heap deletion removes the root, moves the last value to the top, and percolates it downward to restore order.
contents.realLifeExample: It is like removing the strongest player from the top rank and readjusting the ladder below.

contents.title: Traversal Algorithms Using Stacks
contents.definition: Traversal using stacks replaces recursion with an explicit stack that stores pending nodes.
contents.realLifeExample: It is like keeping your own to-do pile of tree nodes instead of relying on automatic memory.

contents.title: Huffman's Algorithm
contents.definition: Huffman's algorithm repeatedly combines the two least frequent nodes to build an optimal prefix code tree.
contents.realLifeExample: It is like tying together the two lightest bundles first until only one coding tree remains.

contents.title: AVL Tree
contents.definition: An AVL tree is a self-balancing BST that keeps subtree heights nearly equal after insertions and deletions.
contents.realLifeExample: It is like keeping a shelf balanced so no side becomes too heavy compared with the other.

contents.title: Trie
contents.definition: A trie stores words character by character so words with the same prefix share the same path.
contents.realLifeExample: It is like a branching dictionary where common beginnings share one hallway before splitting.

contents.title: Graph Traversal
contents.definition: Graph traversal visits graph vertices in a controlled order such as breadth-first or depth-first search.
contents.realLifeExample: It is like exploring a city map by following a planned strategy for choosing the next road.

contents.title: Warshall's Algorithm
contents.definition: Warshall's algorithm updates a reachability matrix to find which vertices can reach each other through intermediate vertices.
contents.realLifeExample: It is like checking whether travel between cities becomes possible when layover cities are allowed.

contents.title: Floyd's Algorithm
contents.definition: Floyd's algorithm improves every pair distance by allowing each vertex in turn as an intermediate stop.
contents.realLifeExample: It is like updating a full travel table whenever a better connecting city is discovered.

contents.title: Shortest Paths
contents.definition: Shortest path methods find the minimum-cost route between graph vertices using path relaxation or matrix updates.
contents.realLifeExample: It is like comparing all route options on a map and keeping the cheapest route discovered so far.

contents.title: Dijkstra's Algorithm
contents.definition: Dijkstra's algorithm repeatedly fixes the smallest unsettled distance and relaxes outgoing edges from that vertex.
contents.realLifeExample: It is like always expanding the nearest confirmed city before considering farther routes.

contents.title: FINDEDGE
contents.definition: FINDEDGE checks whether a specified edge exists between two chosen graph vertices.
contents.realLifeExample: It is like checking whether a direct road exists between two cities on a map.

contents.title: INSNODE
contents.definition: INSNODE adds a new vertex to the graph structure and initializes the related storage for its edges.
contents.realLifeExample: It is like adding a new city to a road map before drawing any roads to it.

contents.title: INSEDGE
contents.definition: INSEDGE inserts a connection between two graph vertices in the chosen representation.
contents.realLifeExample: It is like drawing a new road between two already existing cities.

contents.title: Delete Edge in Graph
contents.definition: Deleting an edge removes the connection between two vertices from the graph representation.
contents.realLifeExample: It is like erasing a road from a city map while keeping the cities themselves.

contents.title: Delete Node in Graph
contents.definition: Deleting a graph vertex removes the node and all edges connected to it.
contents.realLifeExample: It is like removing one city from a map along with every road touching that city.

contents.title: Breadth-First Search (BFS)
contents.definition: BFS visits graph nodes level by level using a queue.
contents.realLifeExample: It is like exploring all houses on one street before moving to the next street.

contents.title: Depth-First Search (DFS)
contents.definition: DFS follows one path as deep as possible before backtracking to explore other branches.
contents.realLifeExample: It is like following one corridor in a maze until it ends and only then coming back.

contents.title: Topological Sort
contents.definition: Topological sort orders the vertices of a DAG so every directed edge goes from an earlier vertex to a later one.
contents.realLifeExample: It is like listing tasks so every prerequisite appears before the task that depends on it.

contents.title: Spanning Tree
contents.definition: A spanning tree connects all graph vertices without forming any cycle.
contents.realLifeExample: It is like selecting only the roads needed to keep every city connected without any unnecessary loop.
